member.name: T:Iris.Server.Delivery.SharedDeliveryQueue
member.summary: A shared, file-backed (Phase 84.6, shared-state scale-out): two (or more) Iris instances over the same origin enqueue into and consume from one durable journal, so a delivery scheduled on instance A is delivered by A-or-B — not dropped — and a single journal is the source of truth for the federation edge.
member.remarks: The single-instance gap. The default and the restart-durable are both per-instance: each instance holds its own in-memory channel, and (for the file-backed one) replays the journal into its own channel at construction. Two instances over one origin therefore each try to deliver the same journal (double-delivery), and — worse — a delivery enqueued on A after B started is never visible to B (B's channel was populated at B's startup, before A's enqueue). The 84.5 single-instance guard made this constraint explicit; this queue is the scale-out half: a shared queue two instances can coexist over.

Model: a visibility-timeout queue over a JSON journal. Each journaled line is a — a plus a monotonic Seq (queue position), a Status (Pending or Claimed), and a claim stamp (ClaimedBy — the claiming instance's id, and ClaimedAt — when it was claimed). The journal is guarded by a cross-process file lock (a separate .lock file opened exclusively); every read-modify-write (an enqueue, a claim, a purge) holds that lock so two instances never interleave a journal edit.
appends a Pending record with the next Seq.
finds the lowest-Seq record that is Pending or Claimed past its visibility timeout (reclaimable — its claimer crashed or is slow), marks it Claimed (stamping this instance's id + the current time), and returns the job. The record stays in the journal (the claim is a visibility change, not a removal).
Records Claimed past the drop horizon are purged (removed from the journal) so the file does not grow without bound.

Delivery guarantee: at-least-once (the same as ). A job is journaled (and flushed) before it is handed to a consumer, so a crash after the flush leaves it for replay. A consumer that claims a job and crashes (or is slow past the visibility timeout) leaves the job reclaimable — another instance re-claims and re-delivers it. The receiving instance dedupes a re-delivered activity by its Id (C-07), so a re-delivery (a job delivered successfully and then re-claimed when its visibility window lapses) is a harmless no-op. The worker's own F-22 retry / dead-letter policy (Phase 17.3) handles per-delivery failures; the queue only gets the job to a worker at least once.

Visibility vs. drop horizons. (10 min) is how long a claim is exclusive: a job claimed by a live instance is not re-claimed by another instance within that window. It is deliberately longer than the worst-case F-22 retry budget (~15 s of backoff across 5 attempts + 5 network calls), so a slow-but-healthy delivery is not re-delivered while it is still in flight. (24 h) is how long a Claimed record is retained before it is purged: after a day, re-delivery is no longer useful and the record is dropped to keep the journal small. Both are configurable per queue.

member.summary: Shared helpers for the follow lifecycle: the Accept/Reject response to a follow, and the Undo of a follow (an un-follow). (Resolving an actor or object IRI from an lives in .)
member.remarks: The builds these on the followed side; the and use the same builders so that an Accept delivered back to the follower references the very Follow that prompted it, and the follower can recognize its own follow.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Http.Proxy.AnonymousProxyRateLimiter
member.summary: Bounds how often a single client IP may use the anonymous proxy seam (GET /ap/v1/proxy/{target}, a signed-out visitor's public remote reads).
member.remarks: The anonymous seam has no actor identity (there is no Basic auth and no site cookie), so the bound is keyed on the client IP instead of an actor IRI. The limit is a simple in-memory counter per IP (no sliding window): the first anonymous proxy reads from an IP within any rolling minute are allowed, and the rest are rejected until the counter expires (one minute after its first recorded request). The counters are pruned opportunistically on each check (expired entries are dropped), so idle clients do not accumulate state. This is a coarse, in-process bound (sufficient for v1); a production host may replace the limiter with a distributed one.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Identity.DocumentDerivedKeyProvider
member.summary: An whose actor→key bindings are derived from the durable actor documents (Phase 84.6, shared-state scale-out — the convergence half).

remarks.para: The default server (, in Iris.Client) holds the actor→key-IRI map in-process only. That is fine for a single instance (84.4's re-derives the map from the persisted documents on a restart), but with two instances over the same persistence each holds a disjoint copy: a rotation on instance A updates A's map, so A's signer signs with the new key, while B's map still points at the old key — B keeps signing with a key that A has moved past (and, once the old key is retired, with a key that no longer exists in the store). The key material is already shared (both instances read the same ), and the actor document's publicKey extension is the single durable source of truth for which key is current (84.2 re-stamps it on every rotation). The only divergent surface is the in-memory actor→key map.

closes that gap. Its (synchronous — the SigningHandler resolves identities in a sync call) reads a thread-safe in-memory map, and is the convergence primitive: it re-derives every local actor's key IRI from the durable actor document's publicKey.id (via , the 84.2/84.4 boundary point, with a #key-1 fallback for a legacy actor) and re-registers it — guarded by so a retired key is not (re)bound. Two instances over the same store converge when each (re)runs : after a rotation on A, B's next refresh re-points B's map at the new key, and B's signer signs with it — no restart, no divergent copy.

This provider is a drop-in replacement for the : it implements the same seam (so the SigningHandler, , and the startup restore path all work unchanged) and additionally owns the refresh. The when of the refresh (a periodic hosted service, or an on-miss trigger) is a separate wiring concern; the provider itself is the convergence primitive.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Identity.IdMinter
member.summary: The server-side authority for minting the id of an object or activity this instance creates (decision 055). The authoring client sends the activity shape (type, actor, object content/references) but not the id; the server mints a collision-resistant, unguessable id in a fixed per-type namespace and stores the object under it.
member.remarks:
The id shape is {actorBase}/{namespace}/{ulid}, where:
actorBase is the IRI of the actor that authors the object (the object is always attributable to a single local actor).
namespace is a fixed, type-specific path segment (notes, follows, …) so the id is discoverable under the actor's own tree and its type is self-evident from the URL.
ulid is a : 80 bits of entropy (unguessable, so no enumeration or overwrite) and a 48-bit millisecond timestamp (lexicographically sortable by creation time).
Monotonicity: the minter uses a so two ids minted in the same tick never collide, even under high throughput.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Identity.KeyProviderRefreshService
member.summary: A hosted service that converges a to the durable actor documents on a fixed interval (Phase 84.6, shared-state scale-out — the "when" of the refresh).

remarks.para: Part 1 of 84.6 shipped the convergence primitive: re-derives every local actor's key IRI from the durable actor document's publicKey.id, so a rotation performed on another instance over the same persistence becomes visible here — no restart. But the primitive is only useful if something calls it. The sync SigningHandler.TryGetIdentity cannot do the async document read itself (CODING_STYLE forbids sync-over-async in library code), so the "when" is this background service.

On host start, and then every (default 30s; a non-positive value disables the periodic refresh but still runs the startup pass), the service resolves the instance's and, if it is a , re-runs RefreshFromActorsAsync over the shared . Any other (the default , or a host-registered ) is left untouched: the service is then a no-op, so the common single-instance deployment and every existing test harness are unaffected.

The refresh is best-effort: a failed document read (a transient persistence blip) is logged and the next tick retries; it never throws into the host. The startup pass runs before the interval loop so a host that registers a fresh (empty) converges to the seeded actors before it signs its first outbound request.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Identity.KeyRotationService
member.summary: Rotates the local instance's signing key for a local actor (Phase 84.2, local key-rotation lifecycle — the follow-up 82.3 documented).
member.remarks: A rotation mints a new RSA key at the next free fragment (#key-2, #key-3, … — the first #key-N not already in the for that actor), stores it, re-registers the actor→new-key binding in the (so the signer — which is already key-source-agnostic, signing with whatever it is given — signs with the new key going forward), and re-stamps the actor document's publicKey extension (the new id + new publicKeyPem + a replaces pointer to the old key IRI, which the read-side RemoteInboundKeyResolver already honors to evict the stale key).

Overlap window. The old key is left in the after a rotation (the key stores are fragment-aware — 82.3 — so #key-1 and #key-2 co-exist as distinct entries). This means a signature made with the old key before the rotation still verifies during the overlap window. An operator calls to remove the old key once the rotation is confirmed (peers that already fetched/cached the old public key can still verify signatures made before retirement; removing the private key from the store only stops new signatures with it).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.AcceptActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles inbound activities: when a remote actor accepts a follow that a local actor (a person or a community) made, the local follow edge is finalized — recorded in the for a person follower, or in the community's follows set () and followers set () for a community follower (both directed edges, mirroring the inbound 's community branch).
member.remarks: On the follower side, a follow is provisional until the followed side accepts it. The (on the followed side) schedules the Accept; when that Accept is delivered back to the follower's inbox (this instance), this handler finalizes the follow by recording the follower → target edge — but only when the follower is local (a person in the actor store or a community in the community store; the local actor's own follow). The followed side's acceptance of a remote follower's follow is owned by the remote instance, so a remote follower's Accept is a no-op here. The Accept's object references the original Follow (by IRI); the target is resolved from that follow (fetched from the local activity store — the follower stored it when it sent the follow). A missing target (the follow was never stored) is a no-op.

Community follower (G-3). A community is a actor, not a person in the actor store, so does not see it as local (the base guard would no-op). This handler overrides the local check to also treat a local community as local, and finalizes a community's follow by recording BOTH directed edges in the community store — the community's follows set (the community → target, the inverse of the inbound 's community branch, driving the community's following collection) and the target's followers set (the target → community, populating the target community's followers collection). This mirrors the 's community branch (which records both edges when a community is followed) and is what makes the follower side of a community-initiated follow (published via the community outbox, gap G-3) two-sided: the followed side's Accept delivered back to the community's inbox finalizes both the community's following and the peer community's followers collections.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.AddActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles inbound activities: the ActivityStreams primitive for adding an item to a collection. When the recipient (the inbox the activity was delivered to) is a local (community), the activity's object (the item being added) is added to the community's member set via the .

remarks.para: Scope — community membership (self-management). Add is the spec's generic collection-modification primitive (AS2.0). Its most common federation use is a server that represents a community's membership as an Add of a member to the community's followers (or members) collection, in contrast to the -based membership Iris otherwise records (F-09). This handler interprets that case: an Add whose recipient is a local community and whose actor is that same community adds the object as a member.

The community manages its own membership (actor == recipient). A community's membership is an act of the community's own management surface: the activity's actor must be the recipient community itself (the community posts an Add through its own inbox, as it publishes Follows through its own outbox — the same self-management gate the community outbox publish endpoint applies to its actor). A collection-modifying activity delivered to a local community whose actor is some other actor is not treated as a membership edit here: only the community edits its own members. (A remote actor wishing to join is a /join request, not an Add it may post to the community's inbox.) This is the authorization Iris records for Phase 19.5.2 (membership management). When the recipient is a local person (not a community) the activity is a no-op: a person's followers is maintained by the follow lifecycle ( / ), not by Add. When the recipient is remote (neither a local community nor person) the activity is not this instance's concern.
Exact-type dispatch. This handler derives from , so the dispatches an Add to it by an exact type match (distance 0) — it does not contend with the (registered for the base type) for the activity.
Idempotent. is idempotent, so a re-delivered Add (at-least-once delivery, C-07) is safe to re-apply.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.AnnounceActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles inbound activities: records the announce in the recipient's outbox (when the recipient is a local actor) and propagates it to the recipient's local followers' inboxes.
member.remarks:
An inbound Announce is an actor re-sharing (boosting/reposting) an object. When the recipient is a local actor (the inbox the announce was delivered to belongs to this instance), the handler:
Records the announce in the recipient's outbox via , so the boost is discoverable from the actor's outbox collection (newest first).
Propagates the announce to each of the recipient's followers (mirroring ): a local follower sees the boost via the follower's outbox on this instance (recorded directly — no cross-instance delivery); a remote follower needs a cross-instance delivery (the peer's handler records it in the follower's outbox on its instance). The propagated Announce (deterministic IRI {recipient}/announces/{objectIri}, to = the follower, cc = the announcer, actor/attributedTo = the announcer) is stored under the shared IRI (the inbox processor's add-if-absent guard keeps the propagated form), and the remote delivery is signed as the announcer ().
member.para: Follower fan-out (mirrors Create). The boost is propagated to the recipient's followers the same way a Create is (see ): a local follower sees the boost via the follower's outbox on this instance (recorded directly — no cross-instance delivery, the follower's followed-feed reads the outbox); a remote follower needs a cross-instance delivery (the peer's AnnounceActivityHandler records it in the follower's outbox on its instance). The boost's id (minted once at record-time — decision 055, see — and reused for every propagated copy) is scoped to the actual announcer, so the propagated form and the original form share the same id: the inbox processor's add-if-absent guard (the 19.3.1/19.3.2 re-delivery loop guard) stores the propagated (addressed) form under that IRI, which the outbox and follower view surface.

The announce is recorded in the outbox and scheduled for delivery even when the recipient has no local followers (the outbox entry stands on its own). A malformed announce (no resolvable actor or no resolvable object) is stored (by the processor) but interpreted as a no-op: nothing is recorded and nothing is scheduled.

Relay fan-out (F-06). After propagating the boost to the announcer's local followers, the handler also delivers the announce to each relay the announcer has subscribed to (the announcer's relays / star set, AP §5.1.3), signed as the announcer. A relay is a remote fan-out server, so — unlike the follower loop — no local-actor skip is needed (a relay is never a local actor), and a relay that has blocked the announcer is suppressed by (F-07) before it is enqueued. This is the delivery half of the relay feature; the subscription half (the local relays collection) is recorded by the Basic-authenticated relay endpoint (Slice 12.18).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.BlockActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles inbound activities (F-07 moderation): records the directed block edge blocker → blocked in the when either party is a local actor.
member.remarks:
Per ActivityPub §5.2.1.3, a Block carries actor = the blocking actor and object = the blocked actor, and is delivered to the blocked actor's inbox (the block is effective on the blocker's side, but the recipient is notified). The handler records the edge in two cases:
Local blocker. When actor is a local actor, the local actor blocked object — the edge is recorded so the local actor's blocks collection (served at GET /ap/v1/u/{handle}/blocks) lists the blocked actor.
Local blocked. When object is a local actor (the block arrived in the local actor's inbox), a remote actor blocked the local actor — the edge is recorded so the instance knows the local actor is blocked (e.g. to suppress outbound delivery to that blocker).
When both parties are remote, the edge is not recorded (it is not this instance's concern). A malformed block (no resolvable actor or object) is stored (by the processor) but interpreted as a no-op. Recording is idempotent (a repeated Block does not duplicate the edge).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.CreateActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles an inbound activity: when the recipient is a local person, records the in that person's outbox (so the author's post is surfaced in their own feed, J-8) and federates it to the author's remote followers (J-18); when the recipient is a local community, records it in the community's local members' outboxes (the "followed content" half of the community feed, delegating to ).
member.remarks: The prefers the most specific handler, so this dedicated -typed handler intercepts every inbound before the catch-all (which now serves and to a community's inbox). The handler therefore owns the recipient decision: a delivered to a local person's inbox is the person's own post (record in the person's outbox, then federate to the author's remote followers); a delivered to a local community's inbox is content a follower published (record in the community's members' outboxes); anything else is a no-op (the activity is still stored by the processor, and an unknown recipient's inbox 404s before the handler runs — the guard is a safety net).
member.para: Why the person's own outbox. A local member's client posts by delivering a signed to the author's own inbox (the client cannot enumerate the follower set — that is server-side state, and ActivityPub has no "post to my outbox" endpoint; outboxes are read collections). Recording the in the author's outbox is what surfaces the post locally (J-8).

Outbound federation to the author's remote followers (J-18). After surfacing the post locally, the handler federates it: for each of the author's remote followers it schedules the author's own for delivery to that follower's inbox via 's actor-targeted delivery, signed as the author (the follower's instance verifies it against the author's key). Only remote followers are targeted: a local follower already sees the post in the author's outbox on this instance (surfaced by J-8), so it needs no cross-instance delivery — the inverse of , which propagates a boost to local followers (a boost originates remotely and must reach local readers). Delivery to a remote follower goes to that follower's delivery target, which resolves as the follower's advertised endpoints.sharedInbox when its document advertises one (F-01) and otherwise as the follower's own inbox. The follower set is this instance's server-side state (), which is exactly why federation must happen here (server-side) and not in the client.

Relay fan-out (F-06). After federating to the author's remote followers, the handler also delivers the post to each relay the author has subscribed to (the author's relays / star set, AP §5.1.3), signed as the author. A relay is a remote fan-out server, so — unlike the follower loop — no local-actor skip is needed (a relay is never a local actor), and a relay that has blocked the author is suppressed by (F-07) before it is enqueued. This is the delivery half of the relay feature; the subscription half (the local relays collection) is recorded by the Basic-authenticated relay endpoint (Slice 12.18).

Idempotency / loop safety. The de-duplicates by the activity's IRI (C-07): a re-delivered (a retry, a restart replay, or — for mutual follows — a peer's re-fan-out echo) is stored as a no-op and is not re-dispatched to this handler. That guard is what stops the two-instance re-delivery loop (19.3.1/19.3.2): only the first delivery of a Create reaches this handler, so the post is federated to the author's remote followers exactly once, never re-fan-out. The outbox write itself () is also idempotent by IRI (F-1911-2), so a post appears in the outbox exactly once.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.DeleteActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles an inbound activity: when the deleting actor is authorized and the referenced object is one this instance stores, the stored object is replaced by a (the AS2.0 "deleted" marker, F-03/F-10).
member.remarks: A references the object being deleted (a bare to its IRI is the common case; an embedded object is also accepted). This handler is the server-side half of "a user deletes their post and the change propagates": the object is not hard-removed but replaced by a tombstone under the same IRI, so a later GET of the object's IRI serves the ({"type":"Tombstone","id":…,"formerType":[…]}), not a 404 — the spec's "deleted" marker (F-10).
member.para:
Authorization guard (138.23). The deleting actor must be authorized to delete the stored object. Two cases are accepted:
Author delete: the actor is the object's attributedTo owner (or a local actor). This is the permanent author-delete case.
Mod removal: the actor is a member of a community referenced in the object's to/cc array (the Lemmy moderator-removal case, where a community moderator deletes another member's post). The tombstone records iris:removedBy so the UI can distinguish the two cases.
A remote actor that is neither the owner nor a member of an associated community is rejected.

Tombstone formerType and iris:removedBy. When the deleted object was stored (an ), its AS2.0 type is recorded in the tombstone's formerType so a client can tell what was deleted. The iris:removedBy extension records the deleting actor's IRI, distinguishing an author delete (actor == attributedTo) from a mod removal (actor is a community member, not the owner).

Federated propagation (the federated half of F-03). After tombstoning the object locally, the handler propagates the to the remote actors that need to see the tombstone — the author's remote followers, the remote attributedTo, and (for a deleted reply) the remote parent's owner — via . A local copy is enough only while the object lives on this instance; every remote instance that holds a copy (via the outbound Create federation) must be told, or it keeps serving the pre-delete content instead of the .

Reply-edge cleanup (F-12). When the deleted object is a reply (it has an , i.e. its stored inReplyTo is set), the local parent → child reply edge is removed from the so the parent's replies collection no longer lists the deleted reply. (The remote parent's edge — if the parent is remote-owned — is the target of the propagation; this instance's edge is local state.) Conversely, when the deleted object is a parent (it has replies to it), the thread under it is collapsed: each child's parent → child reply edge is removed so the tombstoned parent's replies collection is empty (136.9 — without this, a deleted post leaves its replies orphaned but still served under the now-tombstoned parent). The child objects remain stored (fetchable by direct IRI); only the thread listing is collapsed.

member.summary: Handles inbound activities (F-07 moderation): records the directed flag edge flagger → flagged in the when either party is a local actor.
member.remarks:
Per AS2.0, a Flag carries actor = the flagging actor and object = the flagged actor (the flag is a moderation report — it does not sever the relationship the way a block does). The handler records the edge in two cases (mirroring the block handler):
Local flagger. When actor is a local actor, the local actor flagged object — the edge is recorded so the local actor's flags collection (served at GET /ap/v1/u/{handle}/flags) lists the flagged actor.
Local flagged. When object is a local actor (the flag arrived in the local actor's inbox), a remote actor flagged the local actor — the edge is recorded so the instance knows the local actor has been flagged (a moderation signal for operators).
When both parties are remote, the edge is not recorded (it is not this instance's concern). A malformed flag (no resolvable actor or object) is stored (by the processor) but interpreted as a no-op. Recording is idempotent (a repeated Flag does not duplicate the edge). Unlike a Block, a Flag has no feed/delivery application — it is a report the instance stores and surfaces in the flagger's flags collection; the inverse (an Undo of a Flag) is handled by .

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.FollowActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles inbound activities: records the follow edge in the (when the recipient is a local actor) or, when the recipient is a local community, records the follow in the community's follows set; and delivers an back to the follower's inbox in either case.
member.remarks:
An inbound Follow is a remote actor asking to follow a local actor or a local community. The handler:
Records the directed edge follower → recipient: the follower is the activity's actor, and the target is the delivery's (the inbox the follow was delivered to — authoritative for the target). When the recipient is a local person, the edge goes to the ; when the recipient is a local community, two edges are recorded (Resolved Decision #36, extended for F-24): the community's follows set () — the community "follows" the follower, so the follower's content reaches the community's members via the federation path — and the community's followers set () — the follower "follows" the community, so the community's followers collection lists the follower (F-24). A follow addressed to a remote actor is not this instance's concern.
Constructs an Accept (actor = the local actor/community being followed, object = the original follow) and schedules it for delivery to the follower's inbox via (asynchronous — the handler returns after enqueuing; the POSTs it, signed as the instance actor, once the worker pumps the queue). When the follower's receives it, the follower finalizes its own copy of the follow edge — so on the follower side the edge is provisional until accepted (Resolved Decision: the follow lifecycle is two-sided; the followed side's acceptance drives the follower's state).
A follow of a community is not a membership grant: following a community records that the community follows the follower (so the follower's content reaches the community's members via the federation path); it does not add the follower to the community's member set (membership is a separate, local-administered relationship).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.IInboundTagNormalizer
member.summary: Normalizes an inbound note's tag array before it is stored: resolves any @mention / #hashtag tokens that appear in the note's content but are not already declared in its tag, adding the corresponding / Hashtag tags so the note renders with tappable links and carries structured mention/hashtag references (Phase 156, Slice C).
member.remarks: Why. Remote ActivityPub servers (Mastodon, Pleroma, Misskey, Pluralsite) almost always pre-resolve mentions and ship a complete tag array, so this is rarely a no-op. But a non-conforming (or minimal) server can deliver a note whose body carries @mention / #hashtag tokens with no matching tag entry — in which case the note would render those tokens as inert text. This normalizer closes that gap on the server (the object-id authority), so such a note is stored with the structured tags a client (the display-side linkify, Phase 156 Slice B) needs to render tappable links.

item.description: Best-effort: a mention that cannot be resolved (an unreachable peer, a 404, a malformed handle) is left untagged — the note is still stored and the token renders as plain text. A failure never fails the post.

Bounded: at most mention resolutions (WebFinger calls) are made per note, so a flood source cannot amplify a WebFinger DoS through the ingestion path. Hashtags need no network call (the tag's href is the author's-instance search URL) and are uncapped.

Non-federating: the note's to/cc audience is not mutated — the note is not re-delivered to the mentioned actors. The tag is for display/structure only. This deliberately avoids changing federation behavior (and its loop-safety implications) on ingestion.
Idempotent: a token already covered by an existing tag (a mention whose IRI is present, a hashtag whose name matches) is not duplicated.

member.remarks: Never throws: a resolution failure (or a null/unresolvable object) leaves the object unchanged. The object's tag is reassigned only when at least one tag was added.

member.summary: The default : stores the delivered activity, then dispatches it to the registered whose is the closest ancestor of the activity's runtime type.
member.remarks: Dispatch resolves the most specific matching handler: it measures each handler's by its distance (in base-type steps) from the activity's runtime type and picks the closest. An exact type match (distance 0) is most specific; a handler registered for the base Activity type (the largest distance) catches any activity that no more specific handler covers. When two handlers are equally close (e.g. both registered for Activity), registration order breaks the tie (the earlier-registered handler wins). member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.IntransitiveActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles the ActivityStreams intransitive-activity family , , , , and (F-17): acknowledgment-of-receipt activities that a server may emit after consuming another actor's object.

remarks.para: Scope — acknowledgment, no state change. Intransitive activities (AS2.0) are "the actor did something to the object that does not result in a new object" — a signal that the actor read/viewed/listened to, traveled to, or arrived at the object. Unlike the membership primitives () or the moderation activities (, , ), an intransitive activity changes no persistent Iris state: there is no member set, like edge, or block edge to update. The handler's job is to accept the activity (so it is stored by the and not rejected or 500'd) and interpret it as a no-op — Iris does not record a "read receipt" (that would require a new store and has no consumer in v1).

Dispatch. In the library, , , and derive directly from the base type, while and derive from (which itself derives from ). The five types share no single concrete base that a single could be parameterized over, so this handler derives from the non-generic and is registered for the base type, pattern-matching the five types at dispatch. The resolves each activity to the most specific registered handler: the exact-type handlers (, , …) win their activities, and this catch-all (registered before the , which is also registered for ) wins the intransitive family by registration-order tie-break.

Forwarding. Because this handler is registered first for the base type, it sees every activity no more specific handler covers — including the /// membership primitives, which the must interpret. A non-intransitive activity is therefore forwarded to the injected (rather than no-op'd), so the membership family is not swallowed by this handler's catch-all. The is the ultimate catch-all: a genuinely-foreign activity (no handler's concern) is a no-op in its own default case.
Idempotent / safe to re-apply. The handler performs no writes, so a re-delivered activity (at-least-once delivery, C-07) is a no-op by construction.

member.remarks:
An inbound Like is an actor endorsing (liking) an object. The handler interprets two cases:
Local liked object. When the activity's object is a content object stored in this instance's (a local object), the directed like edge liker → object is recorded in the so the object's /likes collection (served at GET {object-irI}/likes) lists the like activity and the object's likeCount reflects it. This is independent of the liker's locality: a remote actor's like of a local object is recorded (the remote actor's like is the object's like, surfaced on the object's own collection), as is a local actor's like of a local object. A like of a remote object (not stored locally) is not recorded here: the edge is recorded on the object's author's home instance instead (the object's liked collection is home-instance-local), so recording it here would duplicate the edge.
Local community recipient. When the recipient is a local community (the like was delivered to the community's inbox), the like is recorded in each of the community's local members' outboxes (delegating to , the same member-recording loop the and use) so the like appears in the community feed. Previously the catch-all owned community Likes; now this specific handler intercepts them first (the prefers the most specific type), so it must delegate to the same member-recording path to avoid regressing community likes.
member.para: A malformed like (no resolvable actor or no resolvable object) is stored (by the processor) but interpreted as a no-op: nothing is recorded. A like of a remote object is recorded on the object's author's home instance (the liker's own liked collection there), not here.

member.summary: Handles the ActivityStreams community-membership primitives , , , and (F-16): an alternate membership lifecycle for a local (community) that a server may use instead of the -based membership Iris otherwise records (F-09 / / ).

remarks.para: Scope — community membership. These four activities are the spec's membership primitives (AS2.0). Their most common federation use is a server that represents a community's membership as an Invite/Offer (an invitation to join) or a Join/Leave (the actor's own declaration of membership). This handler interprets that case for a local community:

list.item: — the activity's object (the invited actor) is added to the recipient community's followers set (an invitation is accepted on receipt).
— the activity's object (the invited actor) is added to the recipient community's followers set (an invitation is accepted on receipt).
— the activity's object (the joining actor) is added to the recipient community's followers set (the actor's declaration of membership).
— the activity's object (the leaving actor) is removed from the recipient community's followers set (the actor's declaration of departure).

remarks.para: Members are followers. A community keeps a single relationship set — its followers (change 221, "Unify Members with Followers"). A Join/Leave therefore records the same edge a Follow of the community would (see ), so the membership state is shared with the community's followers collection and its unified feed.

Recipient is the community (the membership's owner). A membership activity is delivered to the community whose membership it changes — here, the community (the ). When the recipient is a local person (not a community) the activity is a no-op: a person has no member set to add to (membership is a community relationship). When the recipient is remote (neither a local community nor person) the activity is not this instance's concern.

Dispatch. A single cannot be parameterized over four activity types, so the handler derives from the non-generic and is registered for the base type, pattern-matching the /// at dispatch. The resolves each activity to the most specific registered handler, so the exact-type / (registered for /) win their activities and this catch-all interprets the four membership types — and any other activity that no more specific handler covers.
Idempotent. and are idempotent, so a re-delivered activity (at-least-once delivery, C-07) is safe to re-apply.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.MoveActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles inbound activities: when an actor migrates to a new IRI (a Move whose actor is the old IRI and object is the new IRI), the local follow edges that pointed at the old IRI are re-pointed at the new IRI so the instance keeps following the moved actor (F-08).
member.remarks: Per ActivityPub §5.2.1.6, a Move is delivered to the moving actor's followers (their inboxes) so each follower can update its record of where the actor now lives. The handler therefore does not gate on (the recipient is a follower, which may be local or remote) — instead it re-points every local edge that targets the moving actor.
member.para: Person edges. Each local actor in the moving actor's follower set () has its localFollower → oldIri edge removed and re-recorded as localFollower → newIri (). The moving actor's own following set is not re-pointed here (the moved actor's home instance owns that state).

Community edges. A local community's follows set is not indexed by target (the exposes no "communities following X" query), so the handler is constructed with the set of local community IRIs (from the member enumeration) and checks each community's follows set for the old IRI, re-pointing it to the new IRI when present.

Key re-resolution (F-25). The handler clears the moving actor's entries from the outbound RemoteKeyCache and RemoteActorCache (when provided) so the next key resolution fetches the new actor document (with the new key) rather than serving the stale cached one. The key IRI is read from the cached actor document's publicKey.id (via ) rather than hard-coded to #key-1, so a non-standard key fragment is invalidated correctly. The handler then fetches the new actor document to warm the RemoteActorCache, so subsequent reads of the new IRI resolve immediately. A fetch failure is non-fatal (the cache entry is absent and will be populated on the next resolution attempt).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.MuteActivity
member.summary: An Iris-specific Mute activity: the directed moderation decision muter → muted that silences the muted actor's content for the muter (the inverse of which is an of this activity).
member.remarks: Why a wrapper, not a library type. Unlike and , Mute is not an ActivityStreams 2.0 type, so the ActivityStreams library has no Mute class: an inbound "type": "Mute" deserializes to a generic (not an ). Per the coding-style rule against re-declaring library types, this is an Iris-specific wrapper (Rule 6): a thin subclass that pins Type to ["Mute"] and carries the actor (the muter) and object (the muted actor) through the inherited properties — it does not add new properties. The server records the edge from this type, the inbox endpoint wraps an inbound generic Object whose type is Mute into this type, and the outbox-publish path recognizes a local actor's Mute so it federates to the muted actor's inbox (24.2).

member.remarks: Mirrors the : on the follower side a follow is provisional until the followed side responds. A Reject delivered back to the follower's inbox removes the follower → target edge — but only when the follower is local. The target is resolved from the original Follow (referenced by IRI in the Reject's object, fetched from the local activity store). A missing target (the follow was never stored) is a no-op (there is no edge to remove).

Community follower (G-3, symmetric with ) — a community is a actor, not a person in the actor store, so the base local-actor guard does not see it as local. This handler overrides the local check to also treat a local community as local, and undoes a community's rejected follow by removing the edge from the community's follows set — the inverse of the inbound 's community branch and the exact mirror of 's community arm. Without this, a community-initiated follow (published via the community outbox, gap G-3) would be finalized by an inbound Accept but a declined follow would never be undone on the community side (asymmetric with the person path).

member.summary: Handles inbound activities: the ActivityStreams primitive for removing an item from a collection. When the recipient (the inbox the activity was delivered to) is a local (community), the activity's object (the item being removed) is removed from the community's member set via the .

remarks.para: Scope — community membership (self-management). Remove is the spec's generic collection-modification primitive (AS2.0). Its most common federation use is a server that represents a community's membership as a Remove of a member from the community's followers (or members) collection, in contrast to the -based membership Iris otherwise records (F-09). This handler interprets that case: a Remove whose recipient is a local community and whose actor is that same community removes the object from its member set.

The community manages its own membership (actor == recipient). A community's membership is an act of the community's own management surface: the activity's actor must be the recipient community itself (the community posts a Remove through its own inbox, as it publishes Follows through its own outbox — the same self-management gate the community outbox publish endpoint applies to its actor). A collection-modifying activity delivered to a local community whose actor is some other actor is not treated as a membership edit here: only the community edits its own members. This is the authorization Iris records for Phase 19.5.2 (membership management). When the recipient is a local person (not a community) the activity is a no-op: a person's followers is maintained by the follow lifecycle ( / ), not by Remove. When the recipient is remote (neither a local community nor person) the activity is not this instance's concern.
Exact-type dispatch. This handler derives from , so the dispatches a Remove to it by an exact type match (distance 0) — it does not contend with the (registered for the base type) for the activity.
Idempotent. is idempotent, so a re-delivered Remove (at-least-once delivery, C-07) is safe to re-apply.

member.summary: Applies an inbound (the AS2.0 "deleted" marker, F-10) to this instance's stores: replaces any stored object under the tombstone's IRI with the tombstone and cleans up the local artifacts (the reply edge, the author's outbox , and the object → index) that a prior copy of the object left behind.
member.remarks:
A peer signals that an object was deleted on its instance by delivering a — either a standalone Tombstone posted to a follower's inbox, or a whose embedded object is a Tombstone. The serving side of F-10 already works (the object endpoint serves a stored Tombstone under its IRI); this helper is the missing inbound half — recognizing the tombstone and storing it under the object IRI so a subsequent GET serves the tombstone, not stale content or a 404.
The cleanup mirrors : the object is not hard-removed but replaced by a tombstone under the same IRI, the reply edge (F-12) is removed so the parent's replies collection no longer lists it, and the object's originating is removed from the author's outbox + the object → Create index (decision 055) so the outbox collection no longer lists the deleted content. The cleanup is gated on a prior copy having been stored here — a tombstone for an object this instance never held stores the tombstone (so a GET serves it rather than a 404) but has no local artifacts to clean.

member.summary: Handles inbound activities: when the local actor (the recipient of the delivery, i.e. the follower) undoes a follow it made, the local follow edge is removed from the (an un-follow); when an actor undoes a it made, the local block edge is removed from the (an un-block, F-07); when an actor undoes a it made, the local flag edge is removed (an un-flag, F-07); when an actor undoes a it made, the local like edge is removed from the (an unlike — the inverse of the ); and when an actor undoes an it made, the local announce edge is removed from the and the boost is removed from the announcer's outbox (an un-boost — the inverse of the ); and when an actor undoes a it made, the local mute edge is removed from the (an un-mute — the inverse of the ).
member.remarks: An Undo is the ActivityStreams inverse primitive: it undoes the activity referenced by its object. The object here is the original Follow (referenced by IRI). The handler resolves the follow's target from the stored Follow (fetched from the local activity store — the follower stored it when it sent the follow) and, when the recipient is a local actor, removes the follower → target edge.
member.para: Recipient is the follower. A follow is undone by the party that made it, so the Undo is delivered to the follower's inbox and is the follower — the same convention the / use for follow responses. An Undo whose recipient is a remote actor is not this instance's concern (the remote instance owns that actor's follow state), so it is a no-op.

Person vs. community. The person and community stores are disjoint. When the follower is a local person (in the actor store) the edge is removed from the ; and when the un-followed target is a local community, the follower is also removed from the community's followers set () and follows set () — the inverse of the community follow ('s community branch, F-24). When the follower is a local community (in the community store) the edge is removed from the community's follows set (), the inverse of the community's own follow. A missing target (the follow was never stored) is a no-op (there is no edge to remove).

Un-block (F-07). When the Undo's object is a (an un-block), the blocker → blocked edge recorded by is removed from the via — the inverse of the block. The block's parties are read from the original Block (fetched from the local activity store), so the removal is scoped to the exact edge that was recorded (a local blocker of anyone, or a blocker of a local actor).

Un-flag (F-07). When the Undo's object is a (an un-flag), the flagger → flagged edge recorded by is removed from the via — the inverse of the flag. The flag's parties are read from the original Flag (fetched from the local activity store). An Undo of any other activity type (not a Follow, a Block, or a Flag) is a no-op (there is no corresponding edge in a store this instance owns).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Inbox.UpdateActivityHandler
member.summary: Handles an inbound activity: when the updating actor is a local actor and the referenced object is one this instance stores (in the ), the stored object is refreshed with the updated content.
member.remarks: An carries the updated object in its object (either the full updated object, embedded, or a reference to it). This handler is the server-side half of "a user edits their post (or profile) and the change propagates" (F-02): the stored the original object in the , and this handler replaces it in place so a later GET of the object's IRI serves the updated content (not stale data).
member.para: Owner guard. Only the object's owner (the activity's actor) may update it. The handler requires that the actor is a local actor on this instance and that an object with the referenced IRI is actually stored here; otherwise it is a no-op (an update for an object this instance does not hold, or an update purporting to be from a remote actor, is not this instance's concern). This prevents a remote actor from rewriting content it does not own.

Embedded vs. reference. When the updated object is embedded (the common case — the actor sends the full updated object), it is stored directly (replacing the stored object under the same IRI). When it is a bare reference, the handler leaves the stored object unchanged (there is no new content to apply; a reference-only is not interpreted). The updated object's Id must match the stored object's IRI; a mismatch is a no-op (the handler does not silently re-store under a different IRI).

Federated propagation (the federated half of F-02). After refreshing the stored object locally, the handler propagates the to the author's remote followers via . A local refresh is enough only while the object lives on this instance; every remote instance that holds a copy (via the outbound Create federation, Slice 11.7) must be told, or it keeps serving the pre-edit content.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.DefaultDegradedModeGate
member.summary: The default : a thread-safe, stateful flag flipped by the .
member.remarks: The flag is a single read/written with semantics: 0 = read-write, 1 = degraded (read-only). The write paths (the inbound/outbox handlers) read once per request and, when degraded, refuse the write with 503 before touching the store — so a torn read of the flag is benign (the request either sees the pre-flip or post-flip value, both of which are a consistent decision for that one request).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.DefaultReadinessGate
member.summary: The default : the instance is ready once the instance actor's signing key has been registered and is resolvable.
member.remarks:
A freshly-started instance is not ready until its key material is loaded (a file-backed key store reads on startup; the in-memory default is registered by the host before traffic is routed). Until the instance actor's key is registered with the and present in the , the GET /ap/v1/ready probe reports not-ready (503), so a load balancer does not route traffic to an instance that cannot sign outbound delivery or authenticate its own actor. The probe is a fast, dependency-free read (it resolves the identity and key, it does not make a network call), so it is safe for a high-frequency orchestrator probe.
A host that loads keys asynchronously (or from a secret manager) may bind its own (via ExtraServices or an override) that additionally awaits the key-load; the default covers the common register-then-serve model.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.DeliveryQueueHealthCheck
member.summary: A that reports the outbound delivery queue's depth.
member.remarks:
A finite queue is healthy (the worker will drain it), so this check reports with the current pending-job count in . It reports when the pending count exceeds a warning threshold (a backlog is building up, usually because a peer is slow or down), and when it exceeds a critical threshold (the queue is not keeping up and deliveries are piling up unboundedly). The thresholds are configurable via and are disabled (treated as infinity) when left at zero.
It is registered as an singleton so the instance's GET /ap/v1/health endpoint resolves it through IEnumerable<IHealthCheck> without requiring the host to call UseHealthChecks.

member.remarks: Both thresholds are disabled (treated as infinity) when left at zero, which is the default — a host that wants to alert on a growing delivery backlog rebinds these options with positive values. The critical threshold, when set, must be at least the warning threshold (a value that would make the check report "degraded" only at a count above the "unhealthy" count is meaningless).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.DeliveryQueueShutdownService
member.summary: A hosted service that completes the outbound on host shutdown.
member.remarks:
Marking the queue complete (via ) signals that no further jobs will be enqueued; once it drains, returns null and the stops. Without this, the queue would remain "open" after the host stops, and a stray enqueue (or a re-resolved queue) could accept jobs with no worker to deliver them.
The host calls hosted services' in registration order, sequentially. This service is registered before the (see AddActivityPubServer), so its — which completes the queue — runs before the worker's (which cancels the worker's stopping token and awaits ). Completing the queue first means the worker's dequeue loop observes a complete-and-empty queue and exits cleanly (draining in-flight deliveries) rather than blocking on an open channel. The service holds no state beyond its resolved references.

It reports when the worker is configured (an instance actor) and has begun pumping the delivery queue, when it has not started yet (the process is up but outbound delivery is not yet live — the readiness probe uses this to gate traffic until the worker is operational), and when the worker is absent (it was not registered, so nothing will deliver outbound activity).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.IDegradedModeGate
member.summary: Reports whether the instance is running in a degraded (read-only) mode.
member.remarks:
A degraded instance is one whose durable store is unreachable: it still serves reads (actor documents, collections, feeds) but refuses writes (inbound + outbound federation activities) with 503 Service Unavailable rather than throwing, so a partially-down instance degrades gracefully instead of returning 500s on every mutation.
The gate is stateful (it holds the current degraded state), distinct from the (a per-request readiness decision). It is flipped by the hosted service: on a failed persistence read at startup (or a later re-probe) it is set to degraded, and on a successful re-probe it is cleared (the instance recovers to read-write). A host that manages its own degraded-state detection may bind its own (via an override registration); the default is flipped only by the built-in probe.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.InMemoryFederationTraceCollector
member.summary: The default : a bounded, in-memory, thread-safe capture of federation request/response observations (Phase 136.1).
member.remarks:
Bounded memory. The collector keeps at most the configured capacity entries (the most recent). When the buffer is full, the oldest entry is dropped as new ones arrive (a simple ring). This bounds memory for a long-running instance while still retaining the recent window an operator needs to diagnose a scenario. The default capacity (1000) comfortably holds a full interop scenario (dozens of requests) while capping the worst case.
Thread safety. Inbound (the ASP.NET request pipeline) and outbound (the delivery worker) threads record concurrently; the buffer is a and the overflow trim is best-effort (a lost trim under contention is harmless — it only delays dropping an old entry by one more record).
Disabled state. A capacity of 0 disables capture (the collector becomes a no-op), so a host can turn trace capture off without changing wiring.

Iris has no mandatory external dependency by default (the in-memory persistence provider is the default, and there is no database), so a running instance is healthy. This check reports when the instance's options are configured (a with a non-null ), and otherwise. It also surfaces the instance name and the local actor IRI in the result's so an operator can confirm which instance answered.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.InstanceObservabilityHealthCheck
member.summary: A that reports the instance's federation observability: how many stored actors have a resolvable signing identity (the key-store's resolvable-actor count) and the delivery dead-letter count.
member.remarks:
The resolvable-actor count is the number of actors stored by this instance (local actors + communities, per ) whose signing identity resolves through — i.e. the actors the instance can currently sign federation as. An actor without a registered key (a fresh community, or an actor whose key has not been loaded yet) is counted as stored-but-not-resolvable, so the operator can see a gap between "actors on disk" and "actors we can sign as."
The dead-letter count is the number of outbound deliveries that exhausted their retry budget and were parked in the dead-letter store (see ). A non-zero count is a signal that some peers are unreachable or rejecting; it is reported as (the instance is otherwise healthy, but a backlog of failed deliveries is accumulating) and when zero.
Both figures are surfaced in (resolvable_actors, stored_actors, dead_letters) so an orchestrator or dashboard can scrape them from the instance's GET /ap/v1/health endpoint.
It is registered as an singleton (not via AddHealthChecks's AddCheck) so the endpoint resolves it through IEnumerable<IHealthCheck> without requiring the host to call UseHealthChecks.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.IrisDeliveryMetrics
member.summary: Iris's outbound-delivery metrics (Phase 17.2).
member.remarks: A single shared instance (via DI) is handed to the DeliveryService and DeliveryWorker, which record at the same points they already log — a metric accrues whenever the corresponding log line fires. No behavioral change, only observation.

Design (no OpenTelemetry dependency). The counters are plain -based fields (thread-safe, zero allocation, no NuGet). A host that wants to export the metrics (Prometheus, OTLP, etc.) subscribes to and reads — or, once the System.Diagnostics.Metering API is available on the target runtime, wraps this class in an OTel MeterProvider (the recording methods map 1:1 to Counter/Histogram instruments). The metrics are observable in tests by reading after driving a delivery.

Counter catalog.
Enqueued — delivery jobs placed on the queue (cumulative).
Delivered — deliveries that completed with a 2xx (cumulative).
AttemptFailed — single delivery attempts that failed (cumulative; a job may fail several attempts before succeeding or dead-lettering).
DeadLettered — jobs that exhausted their retry budget (cumulative).
Per-label breakdowns (by activity type, failure kind) are in Snapshot.ByActivityType and Snapshot.ByFailureKind. The duration (wall-clock time of a single attempt) is not tracked here — the retry backoff already bounds the time, and a histogram would need the System.Diagnostics.Metering API (a follow-up). The pending gauge (queue backlog) is reported by the DeliveryQueueHealthCheck (Phase 17.1), which already surfaces it to the health endpoint.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.PersistenceDegradedModeProbe
member.summary: A hosted service that probes the instance's persistence and flips the into degraded (read-only) mode when the store is unreachable.
member.remarks:
On host start the probe performs a real read against the actor store (the same seam a file/ or database-backed backs). If that read throws (the store is down or unreachable — not merely empty), the probe:
logs a structured degraded_mode_entered event (with the failure detail), and
flips the to degraded, so the write paths refuse mutations with 503 instead of throwing.
A healthy store (a read that succeeds, even when it returns no actors) leaves the instance read-write. After startup the probe re-checks on a fixed interval (default 30s, configurable via the recheckInterval constructor parameter): a read that now succeeds clears the degraded flag (the instance recovers to read-write and logs a degraded_mode_cleared event), and a read that fails re-enters it. This makes the degraded state recoverable without a restart.
The probe is intentionally separate from (an ): the health check is a per-request, side-effect-free probe that an orchestrator's scrape drives; the degraded-mode probe is a background service that mutates the gate. Both share the same read, but only the probe has the side effect of flipping the gate.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Observability.PersistenceHealthCheck
member.summary: A that verifies the instance's persistence is reachable by reading the local actor record from the actor store.
member.remarks:
Unlike (which only inspects the in-memory options), this check performs a real read against the registered — the persistence seam a host may back with a file- or database-backed . When that backing store is down or unreachable, the read throws and the check reports ; the GET /ap/v1/health endpoint surfaces the fault and returns 503, so an orchestrator can evict the instance from rotation.
It probes the instance actor (): if that actor is not yet stored the check still reports healthy (the store answered; it simply has no such record), because "no actor stored" is a configuration state, not a persistence fault. Only a read that throws (the store is unreachable) is unhealthy.
It is registered as an singleton (not via AddHealthChecks's AddCheck) so the instance's GET /ap/v1/health endpoint resolves it through IEnumerable<IHealthCheck> without requiring the host to call UseHealthChecks.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Persistance.FilePersistence
member.summary: A small, self-contained, file-backed persistence primitive (Phase 16.4, production persistence): a single JSON document on disk that is read into memory at construction and rewritten atomically (temp file + File.Move overwrite) on every mutation.
member.remarks: Why file-backed (and not a database). The codebase's rule is no new NuGet packages without a ROADMAP note + justification, and a relational driver (EF Core, Npgsql, …) would be a new dependency. Phase 16.2 already established the file-backed pattern for the delivery queue (BCL + ). This primitive follows the same pattern for the stores: a production host that wants a real database still swaps in a different implementation behind the same seam.

Durability model. A mutation is durable when its atomic rewrite has completed. In-memory state is the source of truth between rewrites; a crash before a rewrite loses that one mutation (the same window as the in-memory store). Because the rewrite is atomic (write to a temp file in the same directory, then move over the original), a crash mid-write never leaves a torn or empty file — the file always holds either the previous snapshot or the new one.

Concurrency. All reads and writes are serialized by a single per store file, so a store is safe under concurrent access (the server is multi-threaded). The file I/O is async; the critical section is held only for the snapshot read/write.

Public surface. This class and its JSON converters / document models are public so a host can construct the file-backed stores directly (e.g. in tests or a custom host) without going through the aggregate provider. They are deliberately small and stable.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Persistance.FileBackedKeyStore
member.summary: A file-backed (Phase 16.4, production persistence): the local instance's signing keys persisted to a single JSON file that survives a restart.
member.remarks: Each key is stored as its , its key IRI, and its PKCS#8 private-key PEM (the form / produce). On the key is reconstructed from the PEM via / . Because the private PEM is the canonical lossless form for all three algorithms (RSA, EC P-256, and Ed25519), round-tripping through it preserves the exact key material — a signature made before a restart verifies identically after one.

member.summary: A file-backed (Phase 16.4, production persistence): like edges persisted to a single JSON file that survives a restart.
member.remarks: The file holds both directions of the like edge: the liker → likedObject index (the actor's liked collection) and the likedObject → likers reverse index (the object's likedBy reverse index, the per-object like counter — decision 056 (d)). Both are maintained atomically on record / remove.

Document format (backward compatible). The current format is a JSON object {"edges":[...],"likedBy":[...]} where each section is an array of (the edges section is the liker direction, the likedBy section is the reverse direction). A file written by an earlier build holds a bare array of edges (the liker direction only); on load such a file is read as edges and the likedBy reverse index is rebuilt by reversing those edges, so no data is lost. The next write upgrades the file to the object form. Thread-safe (the underlying serializes reads/writes).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Security.HttpSignatureValidator
member.summary: The default . Reads the Signature header, resolves the signing key via an , and verifies the signature via (accepting both signing profiles).
member.remarks:
The request body is buffered (so downstream handlers can re-read it) and, for requests that carry a body, the body's actor field is extracted to bind the signature to the acting actor. The binding is advisory: the result carries when the body's actor is present and parseable; a missing/unparseable actor does not, by itself, fail validation (the cryptographic check is authoritative).
F-21 key-rotation invalidation: when a is supplied and a verification fails (distinct from a missing key), the cached key for the signing keyId is considered stale — the remote actor rotated its key but kept the same key IRI — and the entry is invalidated and the key re-resolved once (a fresh fetch of the actor document) before re-verifying. Because the key is re-resolved by re-fetching the actor document, the owning actor's entry in the is invalidated too (otherwise the re-resolve would re-read the stale document and re-derive the old key, defeating the rotation). This closes the window in which a rotated remote key would otherwise be served stale until the caches' TTL (1h). A missing key (no resolvable public key) is not treated as a rotation signal, so no invalidation occurs in that case.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Security.IInboundRateLimiter
member.summary: A per-peer inbound-delivery rate limiter (Phase 17.4, production scaling): bounds how many signed POSTs a single remote peer may make to the instance's inbox endpoints per unit of time, so a malicious or buggy remote instance cannot flood the inbox with signed deliveries.
member.remarks: The peer is keyed by the host of the signer's keyId in the HTTP signature (e.g. https://remote.example.org/ap/v1/u/bob#key-1 → remote.example.org), mirroring the outbound which keys by the recipient inbox host.

Fail-fast, not blocking. Unlike the outbound limiter (which blocks a background worker until a slot frees), the inbound limiter rejects a request with 429 Too Many Requests when the peer's budget is exhausted. A web request handler that blocks under load is a different failure mode (thread-pool exhaustion, request timeouts); a 429 lets the client back off and retry later (the client's RetryHandler honors Retry-After on 429s).

member.name: M:Iris.Server.Security.IInboundRateLimiter.TryAcquire(System.String,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Attempts to acquire one slot in the peer's per-minute budget. Returns true when the peer is within its limit (the request is permitted); false when the peer has exceeded its limit (the request should be rejected with 429 Too Many Requests).
member.param: The host of the signer's keyId (the peer's identity). Must not be null or empty.
The cancellation token. A host shutdown cancels it; the check returns () promptly rather than blocking the shutdown.
member.returns: true when the request is permitted (within budget); false when it is not (budget exhausted).

member.name: M:Iris.Server.Security.IInboundRateLimiter.GetRetryAfter(System.String)
member.summary: Returns the when the peer's rate-limit window will reset (the earliest time the peer may retry). Used to set the Retry-After HTTP-date header on 429 responses (Phase 18.3). When the limiter is disabled (no rate limit), returns the current time (the caller should not send a Retry-After header).
member.param: The host of the signer's keyId (the peer's identity).
member.returns: The time when the peer's window resets, or when the limiter is disabled.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Security.InboundRateLimitOptions
member.summary: Options for the inbound-delivery rate limit (Phase 17.4, production scaling): bounds how many signed POSTs a single remote peer may make to the instance's inbox endpoints per sliding minute.
member.remarks: A malicious or buggy remote instance can flood the inbox with signed deliveries (a relay misconfiguration, a bug that re-delivers the same activity in a tight loop, or a deliberate DoS). bounds how many signed inbox POSTs the server accepts from a single peer (keyed by the host of the signer's keyId in the HTTP signature) per sliding minute. A peer that exceeds the limit receives 429 Too Many Requests (fail-fast; the request is not queued or retried). A value of 0 (the default) disables the rate limit entirely — the server accepts inbox POSTs as fast as the request pipeline allows.

Why per sender host, not per keyId. A well-behaved remote instance signs all its deliveries with keys that live on the same host (e.g. https://remote.example.org/ap/v1/u/bob#key-1 → host remote.example.org). Keying by host (not by the full keyId IRI) means all of a peer's actors/keys share a single inbound rate budget, mirroring the outbound which keys by the recipient inbox host.

member.name: P:Iris.Server.Security.InboundRateLimitOptions.PerPeerMaxRequestsPerMinute
member.summary: The maximum number of signed inbox POSTs the server accepts from a single peer (keyed by the host of the signer's keyId) per sliding minute. Must be at least 0 (0 = rate limiting disabled, the default; the server accepts inbox POSTs as fast as the request pipeline allows). Defaults to 0.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Security.SlidingWindowInboundRateLimiter
member.summary: The default (Phase 17.4): a per-peer sliding-window limiter. It bounds how many signed inbox POSTs a peer may make per sliding window (default one minute) by recording a timestamp for every accepted request and rejecting (429) when the peer's last maxRequests timestamps are all inside the window.
member.remarks: Peer key. The limiter keys on the host of the signer's keyId (the sender host, e.g. remote.example.org) so all of a peer's actors/keys share a single inbound rate budget.

Thread safety. Multiple concurrent requests may call for the same or different peers. Each peer's state is guarded by its own lock, so concurrent access is safe and a peer never admits more than maxRequests requests inside a window.
Disabled. When constructed with maxRequests == 0 the limiter is a no-op: always returns true (permitted). This keeps the default behavior (no rate limit) unchanged for hosts that do not opt in.

Fail-fast, not blocking. Unlike the outbound (which blocks a background worker until a slot frees), this limiter rejects immediately when the budget is exhausted. A web request handler that blocks under load risks thread-pool exhaustion and request timeouts; a 429 lets the client back off and retry later.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.ServerOutboundTransport
member.summary: Builds the server-side outbound (the innermost transport of an IActivityPubClient pipeline or a DeliveryWorker).
member.remarks:
A plain leaves the TCP/TLS connection phase to the defaults (a 35 s ConnectTimeout in .NET 8+), which is NOT bounded by (that bounds the send/read phase, not the dial). A community feed that follows an unreachable peer (TCP accepted, TLS stalls) would therefore hang ~60–70 s per contributor before the feed could render.
This helper returns a with an explicit (default 5 s, matching the HttpClientTimeout already applied to the feed's outbound client) so a single unreachable peer cannot stall the others. Pooled-connection lifetimes are set to the defaults (24 h / 2 min) to avoid pinning stale connections.

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Services.CommunityFeedService
member.summary: The default : merges the members' outbox activities into a single newest-first feed for a community, and searches that content.
member.remarks: For each member of the community, reads the member's outbox (the member's posted activities, newest first) and merges them into a single **newest-first** feed: items are ordered by (outbox position, then member IRI) — a stable, deterministic merge that ranks a member's newest post above its older posts and orders same-position posts by member IRI. The merged items are de-duplicated by activity IRI (keeping the first, i.e. newest, occurrence). A member with no outbox contributes nothing; an unknown community or a community with no members yields an empty feed. The method runs a case-insensitive substring search over the feed's items' content/name.

Local vs remote members. A local member's outbox is read from the local activity store (no network). A remote member's outbox is fetched over the wire (walking the outbox's pages, capped by ). A remote outbox that cannot be fetched contributes nothing — a single broken remote must not fail the whole feed. When the service is constructed without an (the default), every member is treated as local (the legacy behavior).

Community moderation (19.5.4, apply the community's moderation edges). When constructed with an (the community's own moderation sets — the and edges, scoped to the community being read), a member the community has blocked or muted is excluded from the feed: the moderation is applied on the community's side, so a blocked/muted member's content does not appear in the community's unified feed. A block is a hard exclusion; a mute is a soft one (the membership is kept, only the member's content is hidden). A member the community has only flagged is not excluded — a flag is a moderation report surfaced in the community's flags collection for the operator to act on, not a content exclusion (mirroring the person feed, where only blocks and mutes filter the timeline). When the service is constructed without a community store, no moderation filtering is applied (every member is merged).

member.name: T:Iris.Server.Services.FeedService
member.summary: The default (F-14): merges the actor's own outbox (read from the local activity store) with the local follows' outboxes (read from the local store) and the remote follows' outboxes (fetched over the wire, walking each outbox's pages) into a single newest-first, de-duplicated, capped feed.
member.remarks: For each followed actor the service reads (local) or walks (remote) the outbox's first pages and concatenates the items. The union is de-duplicated by item IRI (keep the first occurrence) and truncated to . A remote outbox that cannot be fetched (404, network error, not a page) contributes nothing — a single broken remote must not fail the whole feed. The merge is in IRI order across follows (deterministic, like the community feed) so the feed is reproducible for a given set of follows.

Block and mute filtering (F-07, apply the moderation edges). When constructed with a , a follow the actor has blocked (per the store's ) or muted (per ) is excluded from the feed: the moderation is applied on the actor's side, so the other actor's content does not appear in the actor's home timeline. A block is a hard exclusion (the relationship is severed); a mute is a soft one (the follow is kept, only its content is hidden). When the service is constructed without a moderation store (moderation disabled) every follow is merged (no filtering). The check is by the follow's actor IRI (the edge is recorded on the actor IRI), so it applies uniformly to local and remote follows.

Reply filtering (117.1, thread-aware feed). Replies from followed actors are excluded from the home feed (they appear under the parent post's replies section instead). A reply is detected deterministically via the content object's inReplyTo field (the primary signal); when inReplyTo is absent, the audience heuristic is used as a fallback (a non-public audience indicates a directed reply). The actor's own replies are always kept in the feed. The threadDepth parameter (117.1) enables inclusion of replies up to a given depth: when 1, first-level replies to followed actors' top-level posts are included; when 2, second-level replies are also included. Depth 0 (default) filters all replies.

Server-side per-actor feed cache. The merged (pre-thread-filter) feed is cached per actor IRI with a 30-second TTL. Within the window, repeated requests for the same actor return the cached list without re-walking every follow's outbox. The cache is process-local; a multi-instance deployment holds one copy per instance (bounded by the same TTL). Thread-depth, query, type, visibility, and source filters are all applied per-request to the cached list.

member.remarks: The actor's own outbox is always merged in (54.17): a home timeline shows the signed-in actor's own posts alongside the posts of the actors they follow. The actor is always local here (the feed endpoint only resolves local actors), so their outbox is read from the local store. The own-outbox items are prepended before the followed actors' items; de-duplicates by IRI (a post the actor made cannot also appear in a follow's outbox, but the de-dup is a cheap safeguard) and caps the result to .

Server-side per-actor caching (feed load feel). The merged feed is cached per actor IRI with a short TTL ( = 30 s by default). Within the window, a repeated GetFeedAsync call for the same actor returns the cached item list without re-walking every follow's outbox (the expensive path). The cache is keyed by the actor's IRI alone (the merge is deterministic for a given set of follows); thread-depth filtering is applied to the cached list per-request (the cached list is the pre-thread-filter union, so a depth parameter can still narrow it without a rebuild). Stale entries beyond the TTL are rebuilt on the next request. The cache is process-local (a ); in a multi-instance deployment each instance holds its own copy (bounded by the same TTL).
